title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 137
paragraphs: Now Miltiades son of Cimon had come to hold Lemnos in the following way. After the Pelasgians had been expelled from Attica by the Athenians — whether justly or unjustly, I cannot say; I can only report the accounts given. Hecataeus son of Hegesander says in his history that it was unjust: when the Athenians saw that the land they had given the Pelasgians to live in at the foot of Mount Hymettus — land given as payment for the wall they had built around the Acropolis in former times — had been rendered productive by cultivation, whereas before it had been poor and worthless, they were seized with envy and a longing to possess it, and so drove the Pelasgians out without any real pretext. The Athenians themselves, however, say that they drove them out justly: that the Pelasgians, settled below Hymettus, used it as a base for wrongs against them. In those days, they say, the sons and daughters of the Athenians regularly went to the spring of Enneacrunus to fetch water, since neither they nor any other Greeks yet had household slaves. When the girls came, the Pelasgians in arrogance and contempt for the Athenians would sexually assault them; and as if that were not enough, they were finally caught plotting an attack on the city. The Athenians, so the story goes, showed themselves better men than the Pelasgians by this: that although they could have killed the Pelasgians when they were caught in the act of conspiracy, they refused to do so, and ordered them merely to leave the country. The Pelasgians accordingly departed and took possession of several older places, in particular Lemnos. The first account is the one given by Hecataeus; the second is told by the Athenians themselves.
